steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on CRISP, a class-aware pruning framework that combines fine-grained N:M sparsity with coarse-grained block sparsity to personalize models for edge devices. Motivate class-aware personalization, explain the limits of existing pruning approaches, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation: universal models vs. users who need few classes; personalization
2. Existing class-aware pruning: unstructured and structured, and their problems
3. Fine-grained N:M sparsity and its limits
4. Coarse-grained block sparsity and its limits
5. CRISP: hybrid structured sparsity
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- ML everywhere: computer vision (cite), NLP (cite)
- universal models on large datasets accurate over many classes, but users encounter only tiny subset (cite)
- deploying to end-users resource-intensive, wasteful
- personalize models, focus on classes relevant to user

2. Class-aware pruning
- class-aware personalization: reduce resources, efficiency, lower carbon footprint on edge devices
- naive: unstructured pruning, weights pruned by class preferences
  - no noticeable hardware gains unless very sparse (\sim 99%), irregular memory access (cite)
- CAP'NN (cite), MyML (cite), OCAP (cite): structured (channel/filter) pruning by user affinity
  - struggle to keep accuracy at high sparsity, remove entire channels

3. N:M sparsity
- fine-grained 2:4 structured sparsity (cite): keep two non-zero of every four consecutive values (Fig. 4 left)
- supported by NVIDIA GPU (cite); theoretical speedup up to 2 \times vs dense
- limits ratio: only 50% of model capacity sparse
- models differ in compressibility: ResNet-50 over-parameterized, easy to prune; MobileNetV2 compact (Fig. 2)
- aim: extend to varying N:M ratios
- still fixed per-layer ratio; can't remove irrelevant layers non-uniformly
- some layers can be pruned much more (\sim 99%) (Fig. 2)
- small subset of classes -> can shrink model proportionally
- varying N:M per layer: more algorithmic complexity (cite), many hyperparameters, impractical for edge

4. Block sparsity
- coarse-grained block sparsity (cite): prune whole blocks, regular access, efficient
- uneven accuracy effects when critical weights concentrated in one block
- Fig. 3: block pruning loses accuracy above 80 % sparsity
- CRISP: decent accuracy (\sim 85%) at high compression (> 92%)

5. CRISP
- novel pruning framework for class-aware personalization; hybrid structured sparsity
- fine-grained N:M + coarse-grained block -> high sparsity, accuracy preserved
- gradient-based class-aware saliency score; select weights important for user-preferred classes
- global pruning; equal number of non-zero blocks per row -> efficient hardware

6. Contributions
- CRISP: accurate user-preference-aware pruning for personalization
- hybrid N:M + block sparsity pattern: accuracy + hardware efficiency
- iterative pruning w/ class-aware saliency; equal blocks removed per row
- ResNet-50, VGG-16, MobileNetV2; comparable accuracy to dense; CIFAR-100, ImageNet
- accelerator design; vs sparse accelerators: up to 14 \times speedup, 30 \times energy efficiency

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning is now used everywhere for a wide range of applications, from computer vision to natural language processing. Universal models that are trained on large-scale datasets give accurate predictions over a wide range of classes, but individual users often only encounter a tiny subset of these classes in their daily lives. So deploying these models to end-users can be resource-intensive and wasteful. One way to deal with this is to personalize the models for individual users and focus only on the classes that are relevant to them.

Class-aware personalization is a promising way to reduce the resource requirements of deployed models a lot, which makes them more efficient and reduces the carbon footprint on edge devices. A naive approach for this is unstructured pruning, where weights can be randomly pruned based on class preferences. But these methods do not give noticeable hardware improvements unless the model is highly sparse (\sim 99%), because of the irregular memory access pattern. Existing class-aware pruning methods like CAP'NN, MyML and OCAP use structured pruning such as channel or filter pruning based on user affinity, but they have trouble keeping model accuracy high, especially at high sparsity levels, since they remove entire channels from the weight matrix.

An important step forward in structured pruning research is fine-grained 2:4 structured sparsity, which keeps two non-zero values out of every four consecutive tensor values, as shown in Fig. 4 (left). This kind of sparsity is supported by NVIDIA GPU, which gives theoretical speedup gains of up to 2 \times compared to the dense versions. The fine-grained 2:4 pattern limits the sparsity ratio, so only 50% of the total model capacity can be sparse. But different models can be compressed to different degrees: models like ResNet-50 are heavily over-parameterized and so they are easy to prune, while more compact models like MobileNetV2 are not, as shown in Fig. 2. In this work we want to explore extending this granularity to varying N:M ratios.

But this approach still puts a fixed per-layer pruning ratio on the model, and this limits the ability to selectively remove irrelevant layers from the network in a non-uniform way. As Fig. 2 shows, some layers can clearly benefit from more aggressive pruning (\sim 99%) than others. Also, since we mainly focus on a small subset of the original class distribution, it is possible to reduce the model size proportionally. However, varying the fine-grained N:M ratio per layer directly adds algorithmic complexity and needs a lot of hyperparameters, which makes it impractical for edge devices.

4. Block sparsity
- coarse-grained block sparsity (cite): prune whole blocks, regular access, efficient
- uneven accuracy effects when critical weights concentrated in one block
- Fig. 3: block pruning loses accuracy above 80 % sparsity
- CRISP: decent accuracy (\sim 85%) at high compression (> 92%)

5. CRISP
- novel pruning framework for class-aware personalization; hybrid structured sparsity
- fine-grained N:M + coarse-grained block -> high sparsity, accuracy preserved
- gradient-based class-aware saliency score; select weights important for user-preferred classes
- global pruning; equal number of non-zero blocks per row -> efficient hardware

6. Contributions
- CRISP: accurate user-preference-aware pruning for personalization
- hybrid N:M + block sparsity pattern: accuracy + hardware efficiency
- iterative pruning w/ class-aware saliency; equal blocks removed per row
- ResNet-50, VGG-16, MobileNetV2; comparable accuracy to dense; CIFAR-100, ImageNet
- accelerator design; vs sparse accelerators: up to 14 \times speedup, 30 \times energy efficiency

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning is now used everywhere for a wide range of applications, from computer vision to natural language processing. Universal models that are trained on large-scale datasets give accurate predictions over a wide range of classes, but individual users often only encounter a tiny subset of these classes in their daily lives. So deploying these models to end-users can be resource-intensive and wasteful. One way to deal with this is to personalize the models for individual users and focus only on the classes that are relevant to them.

Class-aware personalization is a promising way to reduce the resource requirements of deployed models a lot, which makes them more efficient and reduces the carbon footprint on edge devices. A naive approach for this is unstructured pruning, where weights can be randomly pruned based on class preferences. But these methods do not give noticeable hardware improvements unless the model is highly sparse (\sim 99%), because of the irregular memory access pattern. Existing class-aware pruning methods like CAP'NN, MyML and OCAP use structured pruning such as channel or filter pruning based on user affinity, but they have trouble keeping model accuracy high, especially at high sparsity levels, since they remove entire channels from the weight matrix.

An important step forward in structured pruning research is fine-grained 2:4 structured sparsity, which keeps two non-zero values out of every four consecutive tensor values, as shown in Fig. 4 (left). This kind of sparsity is supported by NVIDIA GPU, which gives theoretical speedup gains of up to 2 \times compared to the dense versions. The fine-grained 2:4 pattern limits the sparsity ratio, so only 50% of the total model capacity can be sparse. But different models can be compressed to different degrees: models like ResNet-50 are heavily over-parameterized and so they are easy to prune, while more compact models like MobileNetV2 are not, as shown in Fig. 2. In this work we want to explore extending this granularity to varying N:M ratios.

But this approach still puts a fixed per-layer pruning ratio on the model, and this limits the ability to selectively remove irrelevant layers from the network in a non-uniform way. As Fig. 2 shows, some layers can clearly benefit from more aggressive pruning (\sim 99%) than others. Also, since we mainly focus on a small subset of the original class distribution, it is possible to reduce the model size proportionally. However, varying the fine-grained N:M ratio per layer directly adds algorithmic complexity and needs a lot of hyperparameters, which makes it impractical for edge devices.

Another approach is coarse-grained block sparsity, where whole blocks in the network are pruned, which gives a more regular access pattern and better computational efficiency. The problem is that coarse-grained block sparsity can affect model accuracy unevenly, especially when critical weights are concentrated in a single block. As Fig. 3 shows, block pruning has trouble keeping performance when the sparsity rate goes over 80 %. Our proposed framework CRISP on the other hand keeps decent accuracy (\sim 85%) at high compression rates (> 92%).

CRISP is a new pruning framework for class-aware personalization that uses hybrid structured sparsity. We get the best of both worlds by integrating fine-grained N:M sparsity with coarse-grained block sparsity, so we reach high sparsity levels and still preserve model accuracy. We use a gradient-based class-aware saliency score to carefully select the most significant weight values for the user-preferred classes. Our approach does global model pruning and makes sure that each row has an equal number of non-zero blocks, which makes efficient hardware implementation easier.

Our contributions are the following:

- • We introduce CRISP, a new and accurate user-preference-aware pruning framework for model personalization.

- • We propose a hybrid structured sparsity pattern that combines fine-grained N:M and coarse-grained block sparsity to get high model accuracy and better hardware efficiency.

- • We introduce an iterative pruning strategy based on class-aware saliency estimation that removes an equal number of blocks from each row in the weight matrix.

- • We experiment with three popular models, ResNet-50, VGG-16, and MobileNetV2, and get accuracy comparable to the dense versions across different user-preferred classes on the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets.

- • We design an accelerator-level hardware design that uses our hybrid structured sparsity and compare it with state-of-the-art sparse accelerators, getting up to 14 \times speedup and 30 \times energy efficiency.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine learning has become ubiquitous for a broad range of applications, from computer vision [1] to natural language processing [2]. While universal models trained on large-scale datasets provide accurate predictions over a wide range of classes, individual users often encounter only a tiny subset of these classes in their daily lives [3]. Deploying these models to end-users can therefore be resource-intensive and wasteful. One way to address this is to personalize these models for individual users, focusing only on the classes relevant to them.

Class-aware personalization offers a promising way to significantly reduce the resource requirements of deployed models, enhancing their efficiency and reducing the carbon footprint on edge devices. One naive approach is unstructured pruning, where weights can be randomly pruned based on class preferences. However, such methods do not yield noticeable hardware improvements unless the model is highly sparse (\sim 99%) due to the irregular memory access pattern [4]. Existing class-aware pruning methods such as CAP'NN [3], MyML [5] and OCAP [6] leverage structured pruning such as channel or filter pruning based on user affinity, but they struggle to maintain high model accuracy, particularly at high sparsity levels, as they eliminate entire channels from the weight matrix.

An important advancement in structured pruning research is fine-grained 2:4 structured sparsity [7], which retains two non-zero values out of every four consecutive tensor values, as shown in Fig. 4 (left). This form of sparsity is supported by NVIDIA GPU [8], resulting in theoretical speedup gains of up to 2 \times compared to the dense counterparts. The fine-grained 2:4 sparsity pattern limits the sparsity ratio, allowing only 50% of the total model capacity to be sparse. However, different models exhibit different degrees of compressibility, with models like ResNet-50 being heavily over-parameterized and thus easy to prune, in contrast to more compact models such as MobileNetV2, as shown in Fig. 2. In this work, we aim to explore extending this granularity to varying N:M ratios.

Nonetheless, this approach still imposes a fixed per-layer pruning ratio on the model, which limits the ability to selectively remove irrelevant layers from the network in a non-uniform manner. As Fig. 2 illustrates, specific layers can benefit from more aggressive pruning (\sim 99%) than others. Additionally, since we focus primarily on a small subset of the original class distribution, the model size can be reduced proportionally. However, directly varying the fine-grained N:M ratio per layer introduces increased algorithmic complexity [9] and requires many hyperparameters, making it impractical for edge devices.

An alternative is coarse-grained block sparsity [10], where entire blocks within the network are pruned, resulting in a more regular access pattern and better computational efficiency. Unfortunately, coarse-grained block sparsity can have uneven effects on model accuracy, particularly when critical weights are concentrated within a single block. As shown in Fig. 3, block pruning struggles to maintain performance once the sparsity rate exceeds 80 %. In contrast, our proposed framework CRISP maintains decent accuracy (\sim 85%) across high compression rates (> 92%).

CRISP is a novel pruning framework for class-aware personalization that leverages hybrid structured sparsity. We achieve the best of both worlds by integrating fine-grained N:M sparsity with coarse-grained block sparsity, reaching high sparsity levels while preserving model accuracy. We use a gradient-based class-aware saliency score to carefully select the most significant weight values for user-preferred classes. Our approach performs global model pruning, ensuring an equal number of non-zero blocks in each row, which facilitates efficient hardware implementation.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We introduce CRISP, a novel, accurate user-preference-aware pruning framework for model personalization.

- • We propose a hybrid structured sparsity pattern incorporating fine-grained N:M and coarse-grained block sparsity to achieve high model accuracy with better hardware efficiency.

- • We introduce an iterative pruning strategy based on class-aware saliency estimation that eliminates an equal number of blocks from each row in the weight matrix.

- • We experiment with three popular models, ResNet-50, VGG-16, and MobileNetV2, achieving accuracy comparable to their dense counterparts across varying user-preferred classes on the CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets.

- • We design an accelerator-level hardware design leveraging our hybrid structured sparsity and compare it with state-of-the-art sparse accelerators, achieving up to 14 \times speedup and 30 \times energy efficiency.

References:

[2] Z. Dai et al. Transformer-xl: Attentive language models beyond a fixed-length context. ArXiv , abs/1901.02860, 2019.
[3] M. Hemmat et al. Cap’nn: Class-aware personalized neural network inference. In DAC’20 .
[4] E. Qin et al. Sigma: A sparse and irregular gemm accelerator with flexible interconnects for dnn training. In HPCA’20 .
[5] V. Goyal et al. Myml: User-driven machine learning. In DAC’21 .

[7] A. K. Mishra et al. Accelerating sparse deep neural networks. ArXiv , abs/2104.08378, 2021.
[8] Nvidia ampere sparse tensor core. In Technical report, NVIDIA’20 .
